analysis.one_liner: Forces brand-name drug makers to sell samples of their drugs to generic and biosimilar developers for testing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after referral to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in June 2015, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug makers sometimes refuse to sell samples of their own drugs to companies trying to develop cheaper generic or biosimilar versions, which those companies need for the testing the FDA requires. Without samples, the cheaper competitor cannot complete its application, and the brand-name maker's monopoly lasts longer than the patent intended. This bill would have required license holders to sell requested quantities within 30 days at a market price, created an FDA process for drugs with strict safety distribution programs, let developers sue violators for triple damages, and barred wholesalers from telling the brand maker which competitor was buying.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay for prescriptions, since faster generic and biosimilar competition lowers drug prices. Generic and biosimilar developers gain a legally enforceable right to buy the samples they need, backed by treble damages in court.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the holder of an FDA-approved drug or biological product to provide a product developer with the quantity needed for testing within 30 days, at a nondiscriminatory, market-based price [S2, S3].

For drugs whose safety programs (REMS) restrict distribution, creates an FDA authorization process so developers can still obtain the product for testing, with safety conditions for human trials [S2, S3].
Lets an aggrieved developer sue the license holder for injunctive relief and treble damages, and preserves antitrust laws [S3].
Bars wholesalers and distributors from disclosing to the brand maker the identity of the developer requesting samples, limiting retaliation and targeted refusals [S2, S3].

Lets the FDA waive the single shared safety-system requirement when a generic applicant negotiates in good faith for 120 days but cannot reach commercially reasonable terms with the brand maker [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, who lose the ability to slow or block generic and biosimilar development by withholding samples and dragging out safety-system negotiations, and who could face treble-damages lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill shields license holders from liability for any claim arising from a developer's failure to follow safeguards during testing, meaning someone harmed during a developer's testing might have no claim against the brand maker even though it supplied the product [S3].

The FDA authorization process for drugs with restricted-distribution safety programs (REMS) runs on a 120-day clock and new procedural steps, so access to the hardest-to-sample drugs could still be slow in practice [S3].

A good-faith objection from brand makers is that forced sales of samples at market prices, and the shared-safety-system waiver, reduce their control over how safety restrictions on risky drugs are enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large: the bill's own findings state that sample restrictions extend monopolies beyond the patent term and deter development of affordable generic drugs and biosimilars [S3]. The main cost falls on brand-name drug makers, whose delayed competition is precisely what the bill targets. The liability shield for license holders is a real gap, but it applies only to developer testing misconduct, not to the marketed product.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee the week it was introduced and never came back out for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stivers (R-OH) introduced the FAST Generics Act on June 18, 2015, with five original cosponsors including Democrats Welch and Schakowsky and Republicans McKinley, Renacci, and Tiberi [S1, S3].
Nine members cosponsored the bill in total, five Democrats and four Republicans [S4].
The bill's sole action after introduction was referral: to the Energy and Commerce Committee on June 18, 2015, and to the Subcommittee on Health on June 19, 2015 [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history; the bill died at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they keep the ability to restrict access to their products for competitors' testing, which the bill's own findings said deters and delays generic and biosimilar development and extends monopolies beyond the patent term [S3]. Patients continue paying brand-name prices longer.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: nine cosponsors split five Democrats to four Republicans, with a Republican lead sponsor and Democratic cosponsors including Schakowsky and Welch [S3, S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar them from restricting supply of their drugs to generic and biosimilar developers, including through REMS safety programs, and exposes them to treble-damages suits. The bill's findings state these restrictions extend monopolies beyond the patent term and delay cheaper competitors [S3].

They gain an enforceable right to buy the samples needed for FDA-required testing, at market prices, with a court remedy if refused. Their success is the mechanism by which patients get cheaper drugs [S2, S3].
They become the required channel for fulfilling developer requests and are barred from revealing which competitor is buying, adding duties but also a defined role in the access process [S2, S3].
